correctness.rationale: Within each open-neighborhood twin class, omitting two vertices is impossible. For omitted \(A_i,A_j\) with \(i<j\), the only landmarks that distinguish them are precisely vertices in \(B_{i+1},\ldots,B_j\); the symmetric condition holds for two omitted \(B\)-vertices. Any nonempty landmark set distinguishes an omitted cross-side pair by distance parity. These facts prove the criterion. The recurrence's two state bits record exactly whether an earlier omitted vertex is still waiting for a selected opposite-side class in its distinguishing interval; singleton versus nonsingleton class transitions correctly determine whether an omission also leaves a landmark in that class. A fresh independent brute-force replay on five small class-size patterns matched the recurrence coefficient-for-coefficient. The actual frozen exhaustive verifier was read and checks all canonical vectors through order ten.
correctness.risk: The recurrence is for connected chain graphs in the canonical positive-class decomposition.

value.rationale: A full resolving polynomial is a natural strengthening of the known minimum problem: it characterizes every landmark set, counts metric bases, and exposes precisely how singleton twin classes create nonlocal interval obstructions. The four-state recurrence is a compact reusable enumerative description rather than a one-off computation.
value.risk: The contribution is confined to chain graphs and does not automatically extend to broader bipartite permutation classes.

final_claim: For every finite connected chain graph, resolving sets are exactly complements that omit at most one vertex per canonical twin class and satisfy the two stated same-side interval conditions; a four-state recurrence consequently counts all resolving sets by size and yields the resolving polynomial, metric dimension, and exact number of metric bases.
limitations: The 2015 primary full text remained inaccessible in this run.
